q: Horizontal vs vertical scaling?
o: Horizontal: a bigger machine; vertical: more machines
Horizontal: more machines; vertical: a bigger one
They are the same thing under two different names
Vertical scaling needs a load balancer to work
e:
Vertical scaling (scale up): give one server more CPU, RAM or disk. Simple, no code changes, but there is a maximum size and that one server is still a single point of failure.
Horizontal scaling (scale out): add more servers and spread the traffic with a load balancer. It can grow much further and survives a server dying, but the app must be designed for it (e.g. stateless servers).
r: Vertical = bigger machine. Horizontal = more machines.
fa: Horizontal: add more machines; vertical: add CPU/RAM to one machine

q: Requests have very different durations (some take seconds). Which load balancing strategy adapts best?
o: Round robin: send requests in a fixed rotation
Least connections: pick the least busy server
Random choice: pick any server for each request
DNS only: one record for each of the servers
e:
Round robin sends requests in turn: server 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3... That is fair only if every request costs about the same.
If some requests take seconds, one server can pile up slow requests while it keeps receiving its 'turn'.
Least connections sends each new request to the server that is currently handling the fewest, so busy servers naturally get less.
r: Uneven request costs → least connections.
fa: Least connections

q: What does a CDN mainly provide?
o: A database replica that is placed near users
Caching content near users, cutting latency
Rendering the pages on the server for SEO
Authentication of users before each request
e:
A CDN (Content Delivery Network) has servers in many cities around the world. It keeps copies of your static files (images, JS, CSS, videos) near your users.
A user in Lima downloads from a nearby CDN server instead of your server in Europe: faster for them, less load for you.
Use versioned file names (`app.3f2a.js`) so new deploys are picked up.
r: CDN = copies of static content close to users.
fa: Caching content at edge locations close to users, reducing latency and origin load

q: In the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern, who populates the cache?
o: The database itself fills the cache by itself
The app: on a miss, read the DB and set the cache
A nightly batch job that preloads all the keys
The CDN fills the cache on every single request
e:
Cache-aside steps: 1) the app asks the cache; 2) if found (hit), use it; 3) if not (miss), read from the database and store the result in the cache with a TTL (expiry time).
Only data that is actually requested gets cached.
Downsides: the first request is slow, and cached data can be outdated until it expires or you delete it on update.
ec:
def get_user(uid):
    user = cache.get(f"user:{uid}")
    if user is None:                       # miss
        user = db.load_user(uid)
        cache.set(f"user:{uid}", user, ttl=300)
    return user
r: Cache-aside: check cache → on miss load DB → store in cache.
fa: The application: on a miss it reads the DB, then writes the value into the cache

q: Write-through caching means…
o: Writes go to the cache only and never reach the DB
Every write updates the cache and the database together
Writes skip the cache and go straight to the DB
The cache is cleared on every write
e:
With write-through, every time data is saved, the app writes it to the cache AND the database together.
The cache is always up to date, so reads are fresh. The cost is slower writes (two places).
Write-back (write-behind) writes to the cache first and to the database later: faster, but data can be lost if the cache crashes.
r: Write-through = write to cache and DB together.
fa: Every write updates the cache and the database synchronously

q: A popular cache key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB at once. This is…
o: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
Split brain between two nodes
Hot partition on one shard
Replication lag on a read replica
e:
While the key was cached, the database was protected. The moment it expires, every request misses at the same time and all of them query the database to rebuild the same value, which can overload it.
Fixes: let only one request rebuild it (a lock) while others wait or get the old value; refresh shortly before expiry; add random jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire together.
r: Many misses at once on a hot key = cache stampede.

q: According to the CAP theorem, during a network partition a distributed system must choose between…
o: Cost and performance
Consistency and availability
Latency and throughput
Caching and persistence
e:
A network partition is when servers of one system cannot talk to each other (cables, data centers, outages). In real networks this will happen.
During it, a server that receives a request must either refuse to answer until it can confirm the latest data (choose Consistency) or answer with what it has, possibly outdated (choose Availability).
Banks lean to consistency; social feeds lean to availability.
r: During a partition: correct-or-nothing (C) vs answer-anyway (A).

q: Why use consistent hashing to distribute keys across cache nodes?
o: It encrypts the keys that are stored in the cache
A node change remaps only about 1/N of the keys
It guarantees perfect balance without virtual nodes
It removes the need for replication entirely
e:
With `hash(key) % N`, adding one server changes N, so almost every key suddenly maps to a different server: the whole cache is effectively lost.
Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a circle; each key goes to the next server clockwise. Adding a server only takes over the keys between it and its neighbor, about 1/N of them.
'Virtual nodes' (several points per server) spread the load evenly.
r: Consistent hashing = adding a node moves few keys.
fa: Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of keys instead of nearly all

q: Key difference between Kafka and a traditional queue like RabbitMQ?
o: Kafka cannot keep the messages after delivery
Kafka is a durable log; consumers replay by offset
RabbitMQ is only used for application logging
There is no difference between the two systems
e:
RabbitMQ: a message waits in a queue until a consumer takes and acknowledges it; then it is gone. Great for distributing tasks to workers.
Kafka: messages are appended to a log that is kept for days. Each consumer remembers its position (offset), so it can re-read old messages, and many different services can read the same stream independently.
Kafka fits high-volume event streams; order is guaranteed only within a partition.
r: RabbitMQ = task queue. Kafka = replayable event log.
fa: Kafka is a durable, partitioned log; consumers track offsets and can replay, and many consumer groups read the same stream

q: A message broker guarantees at-least-once delivery. What must consumers do?
o: Nothing, since each message arrives only once
Be idempotent: dedupe by ID or repeat safely
Always switch the broker to exactly-once mode
Acknowledge the message before processing it
e:
'At-least-once' means a message is never lost, but it may arrive twice. For example, the consumer processed it but crashed before confirming, so the broker sends it again.
So processing the same message twice must be harmless: store processed message IDs and skip repeats, or use operations like 'set status = paid' instead of 'add 10 €'.
Confirming before processing would risk losing messages instead.
r: At-least-once delivery → idempotent consumers.
fa: Be idempotent (deduplicate by message ID or make operations naturally repeatable)

q: A 6-person startup with one product debates microservices. The strongest argument against starting with them?
o: Microservices cannot scale beyond a few nodes
Operational overhead: network failures, deploys
They require Java as the only possible language
They are not cloud-native by their very design
e:
Microservices split an app into many small services that talk over the network. That brings real costs: many deployments and pipelines, network errors and timeouts, debugging across services, and keeping data consistent without one shared transaction.
A small team usually moves faster with a well-organized monolith (one app with clear internal modules), and extracts services later when scale or team size justifies it.
r: Start with a modular monolith; split when there is a real reason.
fa: Operational overhead: distributed debugging, network failures, deployments, data consistency across services

q: Which is a typical responsibility of an API gateway?
o: Running database migrations on every deployment
One entry point: routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS
Storing the data of the users of the app
Compiling the frontend assets for the browser
e:
With many backend services, clients would need to know every address and every service would repeat auth and rate limiting.
An API gateway sits in front: clients call one address, and the gateway checks authentication, applies rate limits, terminates HTTPS and routes each request to the right service.
Keep business logic out of it, or it becomes a bottleneck.
r: API gateway = one front door for many services.
fa: A single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS termination and request aggregation

q: A downstream service is failing and timing out. Which pattern stops your service from hammering it and failing slowly?
o: Circuit breaker
Singleton
Saga
Sharding
e:
Like an electrical breaker: after several failures in a row, the circuit 'opens' and calls to that service fail immediately (or return a fallback) instead of waiting for timeouts.
This protects your own threads and gives the broken service time to recover. After a pause, the breaker lets a test request through ('half-open'); if it works, it closes again.
Combine with timeouts and retries with exponential backoff.
r: Circuit breaker = stop calling a failing service for a while.

q: In leader-follower (primary-replica) replication, where do writes go?
o: Any replica can accept writes at any moment
Only the leader; followers copy it and serve reads
Only the followers accept writes, then sync
Writes are sent round robin to all the nodes
e:
One server, the leader (primary), accepts all writes. It sends every change to the followers (replicas), which keep copies and can answer read queries.
Having one writer avoids conflicts. If the leader dies, one follower is promoted to be the new leader (failover).
r: Writes → leader. Reads → leader or followers.
fa: Only the leader; followers replicate and serve reads

q: 1M daily active users each make 10 requests per day. Average QPS?
e:
Total requests per day: 1,000,000 × 10 = 10,000,000.
A day has 86,400 seconds (round to 100,000 for quick math).
10,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 116 queries per second on average.
Traffic is not flat: assume peaks of 2 to 10 times the average when sizing the system.
r: QPS ≈ requests per day / 100,000.

q: Why keep application servers stateless?
o: To save disk space on every application server
Any instance can serve any request (easy scaling)
Stateless servers are faster for CPU-heavy work
To avoid using a database anywhere in the system
e:
If a server keeps user data in its own memory (like a login session), that user must always hit the same server, and if it restarts, the data is lost.
Stateless servers keep nothing between requests: sessions go to Redis or a signed token, files go to object storage (S3).
Then any server can handle any request, and you can add or remove servers freely.
r: Keep state out of app servers.
fa: Any instance can handle any request, enabling autoscaling and easy failover; session state lives in a shared store or token

q: CQRS means…
o: Caching Queries Reduces Storage, a caching rule
Separating the write model from the read model
A query language used by relational databases
A consensus algorithm for distributed nodes
e:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: use one model to change data (commands, with all validation) and a different model, shaped for fast reading, to query it.
Example: orders are written to PostgreSQL; an event updates a denormalized search index used by the order list page.
The read side may be a little behind (eventual consistency). It adds complexity, so use it only when reads and writes really differ.
r: CQRS = separate models for writing and reading.
fa: Separating the write model (commands) from the read model (queries), often with different data stores

q: The three pillars of observability are…
o: CPU, RAM, disk
Logs, metrics, traces
Unit, integration, E2E tests
Dev, staging, prod
e:
- Metrics: numbers over time (requests per second, error rate, latency). They tell you THAT something is wrong and trigger alerts.
- Traces: the path of one request across services, with timing per step. They show WHERE the time or error is.
- Logs: detailed text events. They tell you WHY.
OpenTelemetry is the common standard to produce all three.
r: Metrics = that, traces = where, logs = why.

q: A 99.9% monthly availability SLO allows roughly how much downtime per 30-day month?
o: ~4.3 minutes
~43 minutes
~7.2 hours
~1 day
e:
30 days = 43,200 minutes. 0.1% of that is about 43 minutes of allowed downtime per month.
Each extra 9 divides it by 10: 99.99% ≈ 4.3 minutes per month.
Vocabulary: SLI = what you measure (e.g. % successful requests); SLO = your internal target; SLA = a contract promise to customers, with penalties.
r: 99.9% ≈ 43 min/month; 99.99% ≈ 4 min/month.

q: A chat app needs the server to push messages instantly to clients. Most suitable transport?
o: Polling the server every 30 seconds
WebSockets (or Server-Sent Events for one-way push)
SMTP, the protocol for email delivery
Plain HTTP/1.0 with a new connection each time
e:
Normal HTTP only lets the client ask; the server cannot speak first. Polling ('any news?') every few seconds is wasteful and slow.
A WebSocket keeps one connection open, and both sides can send messages at any time, with very low delay.
Server-Sent Events are a simpler option when only the server needs to push (e.g. live scores).
r: Real-time two-way → WebSockets.

q: Blue-green deployment means…
o: Deploying only on weekends, in a quiet time slot
Two identical environments; switch traffic at once
Deploying to 1% of users first, then growing it
Using two programming languages in one service
e:
Blue runs the current version and receives all traffic. You deploy the new version to green and test it there.
Then you switch the load balancer from blue to green in one step. If something breaks, switch back instantly.
A canary release is different: it sends a small percentage of users to the new version first and increases it gradually.
r: Blue-green = two environments, flip traffic, flip back if needed.
fa: Running two identical environments and switching traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green) at once, with instant rollback

q: What framework do you follow in a 45-minute system design interview?
a:
1. Clarify requirements: functional (core features only) and non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). ~5 min.
2. Estimate: users, QPS, storage, read/write ratio.
3. Define the API and the data model.
4. High-level design: clients, load balancer, services, database, cache, queues, storage.
5. Deep dive into 1-2 components the interviewer cares about (bottlenecks, scaling, partitioning).
6. Trade-offs, failure modes, monitoring, and what you would improve with more time.
- Think aloud, draw boxes, state assumptions, check in with the interviewer.

q: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly).
a:
- Requirements: shorten, redirect, optional custom alias and expiry; read-heavy (e.g. 100 reads per write).
- API: `POST /urls {long_url}` → short code; `GET /{code}` → 301/302 redirect (302 if you want click analytics).
- Code generation: base62 of a unique ID (DB sequence or Snowflake-style IDs); 7 characters ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. Or hash + collision check.
- Storage: key-value table `code → long_url, created_at, expires_at`.
- Cache popular codes in Redis; redirects at the edge/CDN.
- Analytics as async events to a queue.
- Abuse: rate limits, malicious URL scanning.

q: Design a rate limiter for an API.
a:
- Where: API gateway or middleware; key by user ID, API key or IP.
- Algorithms: token bucket (allows bursts), leaky bucket (smooth), fixed window (simple, edge spikes), sliding window (accurate).
- Shared counters in Redis with atomic operations (INCR + EXPIRE, or a Lua script).
- Response: 429 + `Retry-After` and remaining-quota headers.
- If Redis is down: fail open (allow) or fail closed (block)? Decide per endpoint.
- Several tiers (per second and per day), per-endpoint limits, a local in-memory pre-check to reduce Redis load.

q: Design a chat application (like WhatsApp).
a:
- Features: 1:1 and group messages, online status, delivered/read receipts, history, offline delivery.
- Clients keep WebSocket connections to chat servers; a session service maps user → server.
- Send flow: message → server → persist (partitioned by conversation, ordered by time/ID) → route to the recipient's server via pub/sub → push; if offline, push notification and deliver on reconnect.
- Message IDs per conversation for ordering and deduplication (client retries).
- Groups: fan-out on write for small groups.
- Presence with heartbeats and TTLs; media in object storage + CDN; mention end-to-end encryption.

q: Design a news feed (like the Twitter/X home timeline).
a:
- Posting: store the post; publish an event.
- Fan-out on write (push): add the post ID to each follower's cached timeline (Redis lists). Fast reads, expensive for celebrities with millions of followers.
- Fan-out on read (pull): merge followed users' recent posts when the timeline is opened. Cheap writes, slower reads.
- Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities at read time.
- Timelines store IDs; load post and user details from caches.
- Ranking service, cursor pagination, media via CDN, counters updated asynchronously.

q: Design a file storage and sync service (like Dropbox).
a:
- Split files into chunks (e.g. 4 MB) and hash each chunk; upload only changed chunks (deduplication, resumable uploads).
- Chunks in object storage (S3); a metadata database stores files, versions, chunk lists and permissions.
- Upload directly to storage with pre-signed URLs.
- Sync: clients keep a cursor; a notification service (long polling / WebSocket) announces changes; clients pull new metadata.
- Conflicts: keep both copies, or version history.
- Sharing with ACLs and links; CDN for downloads; encryption at rest.

q: Design a notification system (email, SMS, push).
a:
- Other services call a Notification API with user, template and data.
- Validate, check user preferences/opt-outs and rate limits, render the template.
- One queue per channel (email, SMS, push) so a slow provider does not block the others.
- Workers call providers (SES, Twilio, FCM/APNs) with retries, exponential backoff and a dead-letter queue.
- Idempotency keys to avoid duplicates; track delivery status.
- Priority queues: critical messages (OTP codes) before marketing.

q: Design a parking lot system (object-oriented design).
a:
- Clarify: levels, spot types (motorcycle, compact, large, EV), payment, entry/exit gates.
- Classes: `ParkingLot` (levels, gates), `Level` (spots), `ParkingSpot` (type, is_free), `Vehicle` with a size, `Ticket` (spot, entry time), `PricingStrategy`.
- Spot assignment strategy (nearest free, by type) behind an interface.
- Concurrency: two cars must never get the same spot (lock or atomic DB update).
- Show SOLID: pricing as a Strategy, free-spot displays as Observers.

q: Design a distributed job scheduler (run tasks at a given time or on a cron).
a:
- API to create jobs: schedule, payload, retry policy.
- Store jobs in a database indexed by `next_run_at`.
- Scheduler instances find due jobs and claim them atomically (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or leases), then push them to a queue.
- Workers run them, report status, retry with backoff, and send to a dead-letter queue after N failures.
- Execution is at-least-once, so jobs must be idempotent.
- Partitioning or leader election to scale schedulers; heartbeats to recover jobs from dead workers; per-job monitoring.

q: What does a load balancer do?
o: It stores the data of the application itself
Spreads requests over servers, skipping sick ones
It compresses images before sending them out
It writes the logs that the application emits
e:
A load balancer sits in front of a group of identical servers. Clients talk to its single address; it forwards each request to one of the servers.
This spreads the work, lets you add servers as traffic grows, and keeps the site up if one server fails: health checks detect it and stop sending it traffic.
Examples: Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB.
r: Load balancer = traffic distributor + health checks.
fa: Distributes incoming requests across several servers and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones

q: Why does a cache make reads faster?
o: It compresses the database to make it smaller
Hot data sits in fast storage, skipping slower work
It deletes old rows from the main database
It encrypts the data before it is read back
e:
Reading from memory takes microseconds; a database query or an external API call can take milliseconds or more.
A cache stores results you already computed or fetched, so the next request gets them instantly.
The hard part is freshness: cached data can be outdated, so entries get an expiry time (TTL) or are deleted when the data changes.
r: Cache = fast copy of data you will need again.
fa: It keeps copies of frequently used data in fast storage (usually memory), so you skip slower work like a database query

q: In the client-server model, which is true?
o: The server always starts the communication first
Clients send requests; servers process and respond
Clients store all the data of the whole system
There is only ever one client at any one time
e:
The client is the program the user interacts with (a browser, a phone app). The server is a program on another machine that holds data and business logic.
The client sends a request ('give me my orders'); the server checks permissions, reads the database and returns a response.
One server usually handles many clients at the same time.
r: Client asks, server answers.
fa: Clients (browser, mobile app) send requests; servers process them and send responses

q: Latency vs throughput?
o: They are the same thing, measured two ways
Latency: time of one request; throughput: rate
Latency is measured in megabytes per second
Throughput is the rate of errors in a system
e:
Picture a highway. Latency is how long one car takes to travel from A to B. Throughput is how many cars pass per hour.
You can have high throughput with high latency (a big batch job) or low latency with low throughput.
For APIs, latency is usually reported as percentiles: p50 (typical), p99 (the slowest 1%).
r: Latency = time per request. Throughput = requests per second.
fa: Latency = how long one request takes; throughput = how many requests are handled per unit of time

q: Monolith vs microservices?
o: A monolith is always the worse design choice
A monolith deploys as one; microservices apart
Microservices share one database by definition
They are two different programming languages
e:
Monolith: all features (users, orders, payments) live in one codebase and are deployed together. Simple to develop, test and deploy at first.
Microservices: each feature area is its own small app with its own deployment (and often its own database), communicating via HTTP or messages. Teams can work and scale independently, at the cost of much more operational complexity.
r: Monolith = one app. Microservices = many small apps.
fa: A monolith is one deployable application; microservices are many small services deployed independently that talk over the network

q: Why put a message queue between an order service and an email service?
o: To make the emails arrive much faster to users
To decouple them; emails are handled later
Queues replace the need for a real database
To encrypt each email that is being sent out
e:
Without a queue, the order service calls the email service directly and must wait; if the email service is down, the order request fails.
With a queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka) the order service just publishes 'order created' and responds to the user immediately. The email service reads messages at its own pace and catches up after outages.
This is asynchronous communication.
r: Queue = decouple producer and consumer; work happens later.
fa: To decouple them: the order service drops a message and continues; the email service processes it when it can, even if it was briefly down

q: What does DNS do?
o: It encrypts the traffic between browser and server
It maps a domain name to a server IP address
It stores the files that make up the website
It balances the CPU load across the servers
e:
Computers connect using IP addresses (e.g. 93.184.216.34), but people remember names.
DNS (Domain Name System) works like the internet's phone book: your device asks a DNS resolver 'what is the IP of example.com?' and gets the address back. Results are cached for a while (TTL).
DNS can also route users to nearby servers.
r: DNS = name → IP address.
fa: Translates a domain name like example.com into the IP address of a server

q: What is a single point of failure (SPOF)?
o: A bug that is found in a single line of code
A component whose failure takes the system down
The first server that is set up in a cluster
A failed test somewhere in the build pipeline
e:
If your app runs on one server with one database, and that database crashes, everything stops: it is a single point of failure.
You remove SPOFs with redundancy: several app servers behind a load balancer, a database with a replica ready to take over, more than one data center.
High availability is designed by removing SPOFs.
r: SPOF = one part that takes everything down. Add redundancy.
fa: A component whose failure brings the whole system down because there is no backup

q: What is the main purpose of running several copies (replicas) of a service or database?
o: To save money on the cost of infrastructure
High availability: if one copy fails, others serve
To make the code of the service much shorter
To avoid the need to make any backups at all
e:
Machines and networks fail. With only one copy, any failure means downtime.
Replicas keep the system running when one dies (failover), and they can share read traffic.
Replicas are not backups: if someone deletes data by mistake, the deletion is copied to every replica too. You still need backups.
r: Replicas = availability. Backups = recovery from mistakes.
fa: High availability: if one copy fails, others keep serving; reads can also be spread across copies

q: What is a reverse proxy (e.g. Nginx in front of your app)?
o: A proxy that hides the client from websites it visits
A server in front of the app that forwards requests
A browser extension that rewrites requests it sends
A database driver that is written for proxy servers
e:
Clients connect to the reverse proxy, not directly to your app. It forwards each request to the app server(s) and returns the response.
It can terminate HTTPS, serve static files, compress responses, cache, limit rates and balance load.
A forward proxy is the opposite: it acts on behalf of clients (e.g. a company proxy for employees' browsing).
r: Reverse proxy = front door in front of your servers.
fa: A server in front of your application servers that receives client requests and forwards them, often handling TLS, compression, caching and load balancing

q: What is 'system design'?
o: Choosing the main components and how they connect
Drawing the screens of the user interface of an app
Writing unit tests for the code of the application
Installing an operating system on all the servers
e:
Coding solves a problem inside one program. System design decides the big picture: which parts exist, what each one does, how they talk, where the data lives and what happens when something fails or traffic grows.
In interviews you draw boxes and arrows (clients, load balancer, services, database, cache, queue) and explain your choices.
r: System design = the big picture of components and connections.
fa: Choosing the main components of a software system (servers, databases, caches, queues) and how they connect so it works reliably at scale

q: What does it mean when a system 'scales'?
o: It handles more users or data by adding resources
It becomes smaller in size as it keeps growing
It is written with fewer lines of code overall
It is used by only a small number of people
e:
A scalable system keeps working well when load grows from 100 users to 100,000.
You can scale vertically (a bigger machine) or horizontally (more machines).
A system that works for 10 users but collapses at 1,000 does not scale.
r: Scalable = still works when load grows.
fa: It can handle more users or data by adding resources, without breaking or becoming too slow

q: What is a bottleneck?
o: The slowest part of a system, limiting the whole
A type of firewall that blocks incoming traffic
The first server that is set up in a cluster
A security hole that is found in the system
e:
Like the narrow neck of a bottle, the narrowest part decides how fast everything can flow.
Example: 20 application servers that all wait for one overloaded database. The database is the bottleneck, and adding more app servers will not help.
Performance work begins with measuring to find the real bottleneck.
r: Bottleneck = the part that limits the whole system.
fa: The slowest part of a system, which limits the speed of the whole thing

q: High-level design vs low-level design?
o: High-level: components; low-level: internal classes
They are the same thing under two different names
High-level design means a more expensive system
Low-level design means writing assembly code only
e:
High-level design (HLD): boxes and arrows. Which services exist? Where is the data stored? Where is a cache or a queue used?
Low-level design (LLD): inside a box. Which classes and interfaces? What methods and fields? Which design patterns?
'Design a URL shortener' is usually HLD. 'Design a parking lot' is usually LLD (object-oriented design).
r: HLD = components. LLD = classes and methods.
fa: High-level: the big components and how they interact (services, databases, queues); low-level: what happens inside one component (classes, methods, data models)

q: Why do interviewers want you to talk about trade-offs in a design?
o: Every choice has costs; weighing them shows judgment
There is always a single perfect answer to find
It makes the interview last longer than planned
Trade-offs are only about the money of the project
e:
There is rarely a best design, only a best design for these requirements.
Examples: a cache makes reads faster but data may be stale. A microservice split gives independence but adds network failures. SQL gives strong consistency; some NoSQL stores give easier horizontal scaling.
Say: 'I choose X because of Y, and the cost is Z'.
r: Say what you choose, why, and what it costs.
fa: Because every choice has benefits and costs (speed vs consistency, simplicity vs flexibility); showing that you weigh them proves engineering judgment

q: In a typical web system, which path does a user request usually follow?
o: Browser, DNS, load balancer, app server, database
Database, then browser, then server, and back again
Server, then CDN, then printer, then the browser
Browser directly to the database, and nothing else
e:
1. The browser asks DNS for the IP address of the site.
2. The request reaches a load balancer, which picks one application server.
3. The application server runs the business logic and queries the database (or a cache).
4. The response travels back the same way.
The browser never talks to the database directly, because that would be insecure.
r: Browser → load balancer → app server → database.
fa: Browser → (DNS, load balancer) → application server → database → response back to the browser
